title: POC scoping - latency & throughput SLOs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-20 16:00 PDT | Duration 62m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Zenith CTO), Samir Khan (Zenith Lead ML), Priya Rao (Zenith Infra), Daniel Park (Zenith PM)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, we got Ravi from the SE team as well. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Lena Ortiz: Hi Lena here.
[00:07] Samir Khan: Samir on the line.
[00:09] Priya Rao: Priya.
[00:10] Daniel Park: Daniel here.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Great. Goal for today: scope the POC around latency and throughput SLOs, define TTFT vs TPOT targets, workload sizing, and a measurement plan so we can run benchmarks. Anything else to add?
[00:23] Samir Khan: No that's it. We're particularly worried about tail latency at scale and cost impact.
[00:28] Ravi Patel: Cool. Quick context check: you're running a multi-tenant production inference pipeline today with a transformer model family for question answering, right? And you said typical request sizes average 120 tokens input and ~60 tokens output?
[00:38] Samir Khan: Yeah that's right, average prompt 100-150 tokens. Peak concurrent requests hit about 220 qps during business hours.
[00:45] Lena Ortiz: And the strict requirement is interactive experience for customers—ideally sub-500ms for initial response on simple queries but we know generative outputs will be longer.
[00:52] Maya Chen: Good, that helps. Before we dive in, we usually separate TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TPOT (time-to-produce-all-tokens) in the SLOs. Some teams care mostly about TTFT for perceived latency, others need TPOT for overall throughput and cost analysis. Which is your priority?
[01:08] Samir Khan: Perceived latency, so TTFT is primary. But we also care about p95 and p99, not just averages.
[01:15] Priya Rao: Also the tail matters for SLA throttling downstream, so we need TPOT p99 limits for billing and retries.
[01:22] Ravi Patel: Makes sense. For the POC we'll set a two-tier target: TTFT p95 <= 300ms, TTFT p99 <= 550ms for short prompts (<= 150 in); and TPOT p95 <= 1.5s, p99 <= 3.0s for typical output sizes (<= 60 out). Those are realistic on dedicated capacity with batching/kv-cache engaged; hosted will depend on plan.
[01:41] Daniel Park: Can you explain assumptions? Like hardware, model size, batching?
[01:45] Ravi Patel: Sure. We're assuming a 16GB-class GPU for the POC nodes, running a ~7B model quantized to 4-bit or 8-bit depending on perf. We'll use Redwood's continuous batching with a 20ms coalescing window and prefix KV cache for repeated sessions. If you don't enable caching, tails will be worse. Also network egress and client-to-edge time isn't included in these numbers—TTFT measured at the platform ingress to first token emitted.
[02:10] Samir Khan: We have a mix of cold and warm traffic; about 18% are cold sessions where there's no prior context cache.
[02:16] Maya Chen: Good note. For measurement we'll segment results: warm vs cold, short prompts vs long prompts, and burst vs steady-state throughput.
[02:24] Lena Ortiz: What about p50 targets? We mostly track p95/p99 in infra but product looks at p50 too.
[02:30] Ravi Patel: We'll capture p50 as well. But SLOs will be p95/p99.
[02:34] Priya Rao: About workload sizing—how do we pick qps for the POC? Our peak is 220 qps but we want to validate both 1x peak and 3x burst to ensure autoscaling.
[02:43] Maya Chen: Recommendation: run load tests at 1x baseline (220 qps), 2x (440 qps) and a 3x short burst (660 qps) for 5-10m to validate autoscale behavior. Also run a long soak at baseline for 60-90m to see cache warming.
[02:58] Samir Khan: That soak aligns with our long-running jobs.
[03:01] Ravi Patel: We'll plan benchmarks: step 1 warm/cold microbench with isolated single-connection requests to measure base TTFT; step 2 concurrency sweep for throughput vs latency curves; step 3 burst/soak with your real prompt mix. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and token/s cost.
[03:17] Daniel Park: How many samples per test for p99 to be statistically meaningful?
[03:21] Ravi Patel: For p99 you want thousands of samples— the recommendation is at least 10k requests per test condition. For p99 confidence intervals, more is better. We'll capture histograms and export to your observability.
[03:33] Priya Rao: Who will run the load generator? We prefer to run from our VPC to avoid network artifacts.
[03:37] Maya Chen: For Private/ Dedicated POC we can deploy a load harness in your VPC. For hosted, we use a public load generator but try to run from a region near your infra.
[03:46] Lena Ortiz: We're leaning Dedicated for the POC.
[03:48] Maya Chen: Noted. Security checklist: SSO, SAML, KMS for keys, audit logs—Priya, any must-haves?
[03:56] Priya Rao: KMS integration (we use HSM-backed keys), SOC2 compliance report, and per-token logging disabled by default.
[04:03] Maya Chen: We'll share our security pack.
[04:06] Samir Khan: Back to metrics: define TTFT precisely in the plan so everyone measures same.
[04:11] Ravi Patel: TTFT = time from request ingress at Redwood edge (post-auth) to emission of first token by the model. TPOT = time from ingress to final token emitted. We'll also measure token emission rate and tokens per second. We'll instrument client-to-edge separately if you need end-to-end user perceived latency.
[04:28] Lena Ortiz: Good. How do we account for streaming (server-sent events) vs batch responses?
[04:33] Ravi Patel: For streaming we'll use first-byte event as TTFT. For batch non-streaming we'll measure first token in the assembled response. We'll note behavior differences in results.
[04:43] Daniel Park: We need per-route SLOs. Some internal endpoints are OK at 800ms p95, whereas customer-facing chat needs 300ms.
[04:50] Maya Chen: We'll support per-route SLOs in the config and run measurements grouped by route.
[04:55] Samir Khan: For the POC timeline—what's realistic?
[04:58] Maya Chen: Typical POC: onboarding + security review 1 week, infra setup + load harness 1 week, benchmarks 1 week, results review + tuning 1 week. So 3-5 weeks total. If procurement or legal adds delay that extends timeline.
[05:12] Priya Rao: We have a procurement freeze last week of month, might push approvals 1 week.
[05:16] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll plan for 4 weeks and target completion before your internal milestone on 2026-09-20.
[05:24] Ravi Patel: Measurement plan specifics:
- Test conditions: warm/cold, baseline/2x/3x burst, short/long prompts.
- Metrics: TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, queue depth, batch sizes, cache hit rate.
- Sample size: >=10k requests per condition; for burst tests shorter but repeat 3 runs.
- Instrumentation: export to your Prometheus/Datadog via our integrations; raw logs in S3 if needed.
[05:46] Lena Ortiz: Do you provide the prompt mix generator or should we supply representative prompts?
[05:50] Ravi Patel: We can supply a prompt mix template and you can plug in representative prompts. For confidentiality, you can send obfuscated prompts or we can run on-site with private deployment.
[05:59] Samir Khan: We'll send a sample corpus of 500 prompts covering short/long and different intents.
[06:04] Maya Chen: Great. On success criteria we'll define quantitative pass/fail and qualitative acceptance. Quantitative: TTFT p95 <= 300ms and p99 <= 550ms for customer-facing route at baseline; TPOT p99 <= 3.0s. Throughput: maintain 220 qps steady with <5% request errors and acceptable cost per 1M tokens. Qualitative: no regression in output quality vs your baseline eval set.
[06:26] Daniel Park: How do you measure quality regression?
[06:29] Ravi Patel: We'll run your eval set through both our POC model and your current baseline and compute a set of metrics (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE for structured outputs or human eval for correctness). We'll also sample side-by-side for product team to review.
[06:43] Priya Rao: Any gotchas we should know?
[06:45] Ravi Patel: Cold cache tests can blow up TTFT; plan to separate them. Also autoscaling cold-start latency can be 8-20s depending on GPU warmup if you scale the worker pool. We'll show warm node pools if you need <1s cold behavior. Networking and TLS termination near edge can add 50-100ms.
[07:02] Lena Ortiz: If we need <200ms p95 we likely need pinned capacity and tuned quantization, correct?
[07:09] Ravi Patel: Yes, sub-200ms p95 is aggressive and usually requires pinned dedicated capacity, optimized kernels, and short-token responses. We'll prototype that but set realistic expectations.
[07:19] Maya Chen: Let's capture next steps and action items.
[07:22] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to share security pack and POC runbook, provide prompt mix template and measurement plan. Zenith to provide sample corpus (500 prompts), confirm procurement timeline, and grant a small VPC test environment for load harness. We'll schedule baseline test the week of 2026-08-31.
[07:39] Samir Khan: Sounds good.
[07:41] Lena Ortiz: One more: can you include cost estimates for Dedicated vs Hosted for the POC?
[07:46] Maya Chen: We'll include a pricing sheet in the follow-up.
[07:49] Daniel Park: Ok thanks all.
[07:51] Maya Chen: Thank you, we'll share notes and schedule.

Transcript notes: occasional mistranscriptions: "KV cache" appears as "K-V cash" in auto-text; "TTFT" sometimes spoken as "T-T-F-T"; speaker labels auto-attributed in sections.
summary: Redwood and Zenith AI scoped a 4-week POC focused on latency and throughput SLOs. Primary goals: define TTFT and TPOT targets (TTFT p95<=300ms p99<=550ms; TPOT p95<=1.5s p99<=3.0s), plan benchmarks (warm vs cold, 1x/2x/3x concurrency), measurement instrumentation, and security requirements. Zenith will provide a 500-prompt corpus and VPC test environment; Redwood will share security pack, runbook, and pricing. POC timeline target: baseline tests week of 2026-08-31 and completion before 2026-09-20.

Redwood share pricing sheet and measurement plan (Ravi)
Zenith to send 500 prompt sample corpus (Samir)
